title: Are any two prime numbers co-prime?
description: Two different primes are tried, and then the same prime twice. The rows of primes and the lists of factors show when a claim about primes holds.
teaching_notes: One idea: two different primes share no prime, but the same prime twice shares itself. Watch for students who accept a claim from a few examples without trying the same prime twice.

video_script.why: The child tests a claim about primes by trying two different primes and then the same prime twice, and comparing their rows of primes.
video_script.substitution: the book's own claim, and the primes two, three and eleven as test cases
video_script.anchor: two rows made of one prime each, with the common prime ringed when the two primes are the same
video_script.payoff_line: Two different primes are co-prime, but the same prime twice is not

final_answer.value: Yes for two different primes; not for the same prime twice, such as 3 and 3.
final_answer.spoken: right for two different primes, but not for the same prime twice

names.Leeza: the child who says any two prime numbers are co-prime

hold_back: not for the same prime twice
maths_rules: two different primes, such as 2 and 3 or 3 and 11, have rows with no common prime, so they are co-prime
factors of 2 are 1 and 2, factors of 3 are 1 and 3, the only common factor is 1
the same prime twice, such as 3 and 3, has the prime 3 in both rows, so they are not co-prime
factors of 3 and 3 are 1 and 3, so the common factors are 1 and 3
video_script.design: Each prime is a row of one prime. Pairs of different primes are compared first, and then a prime paired with itself.
